# The Docker client object


{{autogenerated}}

## Default CLI deadlines

`DockerClient(default_timeout=30)` applies a 30-second deadline to each local
CLI launch. The default is `None`, which leaves launches unbounded. Where a
method accepts `timeout`, `None` inherits the client default and a positive
explicit value replaces it. The selected value is captured when each child
starts, including lazy archive exports and queued transfers.

Expiry kills and reaps the local CLI, including when archive consumption is
paused or an archive producer is blocked. The timeout is reported when caller
execution resumes; arbitrary Python iterator code cannot be interrupted. This
does not guarantee descendant cleanup or roll back daemon-side operations.

## About multithreading and multiprocessing

Behind the scenes, pywhales calls the Docker command line interface with
subprocess. The pywhales client does not store any intermediate state so it's safe
to use with multithreading. 

The Docker objects store some intermediate states (the attributes 
that you would normally get with `docker ... inspect`but no logic in 
the codebase depends on those attributes. They're just here so that users can look at them. 
So you can share them between process/threads and pickle containers, images, networks...

The Docker daemon works with its own objects internally and handles concurrent and conflicting requests. 
For example, if you create two containers with the same name from different threads, only one will 
succeed. If you pull the same docker image from multiple processes/threads, the Docker daemon will 
only pull the image and layers once.

Just be careful with some scenario similar to this one

```
Thread 1: my_container = docker.run(..., detach=True)
...
# my_container finishes
...
Thread 2: docker.container.prune()
...
Thread 1: docker.logs(my_container)  # will fail because the container was removed by thread 2
```

In the end, unless you use this type of logic in your code, 
pywhales is safe to use with multithreading and multiprocessing.


## The Docker CLI

pywhales needs the Docker CLI to work (unlike docker-py).
Most of the time, users already have the CLI installed on their machines. It's possible to 
verify that the CLI is there by doing `docker --help` in the command line.

Sometimes, the CLI might not be available on the system, it can happen if you want to control
Docker from within a container with `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock`, or if you
want to connect to a remote daemon with the `host` argument.

Instructions for installing Docker can be found at <https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/>.
Note that if connecting to Docker remotely then a local Docker daemon (`dockerd`) is not needed.

Previously, when using python-on-whales, the Docker CLI was downloaded automatically, but
this functionality was removed under <https://github.com/gabrieldemarmiesse/python-on-whales/pull/633>.


### Handling an unavailable client

Trying to use pywhales when it cannot find a Docker client binary
will trigger a `pywhales.ClientNotFoundError`. You can use a try-except around
a first `docker.ps()` call to handle the case when pywhales won't work.

## Bounded inspection and inventory

Choose an `InspectionPolicy` for your workload. All three limits are required
positive integers; booleans aren't accepted and there are no deployment defaults.
The values below are illustrative, not recommendations for your deployment.

```python
from threading import Event
from time import monotonic

from pywhales import (
    DockerClient,
    InspectionPolicy,
    InventoryRequest,
    capture_inventory,
    observation,
)
from pywhales.client_config import bulk_reload

client = DockerClient()
handle = client.container.inspect("name")
policy = InspectionPolicy(
    max_references=100,
    max_argv_bytes=32768,
    max_response_bytes=1048576,
)
event = Event()
remaining = 30.0  # seconds chosen by the operator

with observation(policy, deadline=monotonic() + remaining, cancel=event):
    snapshot = capture_inventory(
        [
            InventoryRequest(
                kind="container",
                references=("name", "name"),
                client_config=client.client_config,
            ),
            handle,
        ],
        policy=policy,
    )
    bulk_reload([handle], policy=policy)
```

`capture_inventory` returns an `InventorySnapshot` whose `records` are a tuple;
`started_at` and `finished_at` are UTC timestamps delimiting the capture. Each
`InventoryRecord` has frozen `kind` and `id` fields and a typed, deeply copied
`payload`. Callers may mutate a payload, and each duplicate has its own detached
copy. Reading a record doesn't inspect or change a live handle.

Supported kinds are `container`, `image`, `network`, `volume`, `node`,
`service`, `config`, `secret`, `task`, `plugin`, and `context`. Aliases follow
the existing rules for their resource namespace. Request order and duplicates
are retained. Handles use their exact originating client configuration; equal
but distinct configuration objects aren't merged. Empty input launches no CLI.
Capture stages and validates all results before returning and never changes the
original handle caches. `bulk_reload` also stages all groups before publishing;
its publication isn't atomic to concurrent readers.

`observation` applies to synchronous list and inspect calls that execute through
`run`. Its deadline is an absolute monotonic time, and nested scopes can only
tighten the active limits. The scope applies to the current context; it doesn't
automatically propagate to worker threads. Interactive, uncaptured, and stdin
modes aren't supported inside `run`.

Streams and archive transfers started inside a scope honor it as well: log and
progress streams, `docker.load`, and `docker.save`. They check cancellation and
the argv and environment limits before the local CLI starts, keep the scope's
deadline and cancel tokens after the `with` block exits, and, when the scope
ends first, kill and reap the CLI and raise `ObservationTimeout` or
`ObservationCancelled` from iteration. A lazy `save` takes the scope active at
its first iteration. A per-call `timeout` that is strictly earlier than the
scope's deadline still raises `DockerTimeout`. Multi-image `pull` and `push`
run each pool task in its own copy of the calling context, so they behave like
a single image. Response-byte budgets don't count streamed or archive payloads. An explicit capture policy still inherits an
outer deadline and cancellation. `bulk_reload(handles, policy=policy)` is
bounded; when the policy is omitted, an active observation scope applies. Outside
such a scope, the existing default behavior is unchanged.

The reference limit applies to each inspect invocation, not to the overall list
or number of records. The argv limit accounts for the complete encoded command
and native platform limits. The response limit counts combined captured stdout
and stderr as raw bytes per invocation. `ObservationLimitError`, observation
cancellation, and observation timeout are distinct failures; the existing
selected-launch `DockerTimeout` remains unchanged. A timeout or cancellation
kills and reaps the local CLI child only.
It doesn't roll back daemon operations, and the operating system's process
creation step can't be interrupted.

These limits don't bound the complete result, staged models, decoded JSON, deep
copies, Python object overhead, or aggregate process memory. A capture isn't a
transactional daemon snapshot: concurrent changes can produce observations from
different moments. There are no automatic retries or capacity guarantees.
